title: The hypertrophy series: applying reps in reserve while minimizing tonnage loss
summary: NH recommends leaving exactly one rep in reserve on strength work at the start of a session for longevity and mental reasons, while admitting it sacrifices the highest-quality rep. Leaving more than one rep is sandbagging. Accessories and volume work should go to one rep short of failure with no reserve.
claims: On strength work at the start of the session, shave one rep off every set, because that last rep is the one most likely to injure you
Using one RIR on strength work cut his strength-work injuries to almost zero
The downside of RIR: the shaved rep is the highest-intensity, highest-quality tonnage of the set
Nothing kills a session more than failing a rep; repeated failed reps mean your programming is broken
Train close to failure but never actually fail in the gym; repeated failures build a loser's mindset and mental plateaus
RIR is a long-term investment: you may give up ~300 lb of quality tonnage now but avoid plateaus and injuries and overtake all-out lifters
Leave one rep in reserve, never two or more; tonnage loss grows exponentially because each rep before the last is also high intensity
Needing more than one RIR means either poor weight selection or sandbagging
Sandbagging is fine for muscles you don't want to grow now, as a deliberate tonnage sacrifice redirecting effort elsewhere
RIR lets you progress faster because the reserved rep would be the least technical, most ground-out rep with form breakdown
Knowing you could have gotten the extra rep builds confidence, making next week's target easy
Outside opening strength work, don't use RIR: take accessories and volume work to one rep short of failure, adjusting rep ranges so the last rep is that close
Shaving a rep from eight accessory sets loses more reps than three strength sets, and accessories are low injury risk, so RIR there makes no sense
